title: Recurrent Ischaemic Stroke Secondary to Cerebral Small Vessel Vasculopathy From Clonal B-Cell Lymphomatosis of Marginal Zone Origin
case_prompt:
A 54-year-old Chinese man under active surveillance for clonal B-cell lymphocytosis of marginal zone origin (CBL-MZ) presented initially with livedo reticularis. Skin biopsy showed perivascular IgM deposition and fibrin thrombi; bone marrow biopsy identified a CD5– CD10– kappa-expressing B-cell clone, and serum IgM-k paraprotein was 3.9 g/L. CT of neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.

Nine months after diagnosis, he experienced episodic nonpositional giddiness and transient visual darkening. Neurologic and ocular exams were normal; brain MRI demonstrated chronic subcortical infarcts, attributed to increased plasma viscosity. He was managed with aspirin.

Seven months later, he was admitted for daily 1-minute episodes of giddiness and visual blurring. He denied systemic symptoms; exam remained unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including lipid and glucose profiles, and hematologic parameters were unchanged. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed multiple acute and subacute subcortical infarcts in a deep perforator distribution. MRA and CT angiography showed no large-vessel stenosis or occlusion.

A workup for stroke etiology was unremarkable: tests for antiphospholipid antibodies, protein C and S, antithrombin III, and prothrombin G20210A mutation were negative. Extended cardiac monitoring and transthoracic echocardiography were normal; transesophageal echocardiography revealed a 7-mm filamentous aortic-valve mass and a small patent foramen ovale without shunt. Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography detected no microembolic signals.

CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (19 WBC/µL) and elevated protein. Microbiologic studies (HSV-1/2 PCR, Gram stain and culture, fungal and AFB studies) were negative. Oligoclonal bands were absent; CSF cytology, flow cytometry, and MYD88 mutation analysis were negative.

His strokes were classified as cryptogenic, and he was started on antiplatelet and statin therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cardioembolic source was unlikely — “cardiac embolism tends to result in larger territorial or cortical infarcts, no microembolic signals were demonstrated on monitoring of the MCAs, and no benefit was seen despite therapeutic anticoagulation.”
2. Malignancy-related prothrombosis was excluded — “evaluation for systemic causes of prothrombosis was negative, d-dimer was not significantly elevated … and infarcts in malignancy-related prothrombosis usually appear embolic in multiple territories, including the cortices, instead of the deep subcortical and basal ganglia location seen in our patient.”
3. Lipohyalinosis from hypertension was unlikely — “Typical arteriosclerosis secondary to lipohyalinosis from chronic hypertension results in single infarcts in the distribution of penetrating cerebral arteries, unlike our patient who had recurrent multifocal infarcts despite optimisation of cardiovascular risk factors.”
4. Infectious etiologies were excluded — “Infectious and iatrogenic aetiologies were excluded from CSF microbiology and the absence of previous exposure to inciting agents respectively.”
5. Genetic arteriopathy was unlikely — “He had no family history of cerebrovascular disease, and the rapid clinical progression made a genetic cause unlikely.”
6. Systemic vasculitis was excluded — “There were no features of systemic autoimmunity, and antibodies for systemic vasculitis were absent.”
7. Sneddon syndrome was unlikely — “However, unlike our patient, the CSF in Sneddon syndrome is usually normal, and there tends to be a response to anticoagulation.”
8. Intravascular lymphoma was excluded — “the lesions in intravascular lymphoma are typically cortical, and there was no evidence of aggressive transformation of the clonal B cells found on repeated CSF samplings.”
9. Primary CNS angiitis (PACNS) was excluded — “PACNS was excluded as clonal B-cells were found in the CSF.”
10. Hyperviscosity syndrome was unlikely — “ischaemic strokes are rare, as viscosity is highest in small venules. The diagnosis is made with significantly elevated monoclonal paraprotein concentrations or serum viscosity, not seen in our patient.”
11. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis was excluded — “and is confirmed by the presence of cryoglobulins in the serum, which was repeatedly negative in our patient.”
12. Bing–Neel syndrome and CNS myeloma were unlikely — “… rather than infarcts, brain MRI may show contrast enhancement and/or thickening of the meninges, or focal contrast-enhancing lesions in the cerebral parenchyma, which were not observed in our patient.”
